title: Watai: a private AI assistant of my own
summary: A private, Azure-backed personal AI assistant I built so my data and credentials stay under my control.

body.markdown: I wanted my own personal AI solution where my data remains private. That was the starting point for Watai: a ChatGPT-style web app powered by my own Azure OpenAI endpoint, with the assistant experience I wanted without handing the whole workflow to someone else's consumer product.

The project is a React and Vite progressive web app with an Azure Functions backend. The frontend is published through GitHub Pages, while the backend owns the durable work: generation runs, encrypted credentials, sync, assets, and memory. The goal is simple from the user's side: sign in, configure an Azure OpenAI endpoint once, and use a private AI workspace across devices.

items.heading: Built with
items.subtext: React, Vite, Azure Functions, Cosmos DB, Blob Storage, Key Vault

items.heading: Status
items.subtext: Public repo and live GitHub Pages frontend

body.markdown: The privacy decision shaped the product more than any individual feature. Watai uses the user's own Azure OpenAI configuration. In the current server-authoritative direction, credentials are stored encrypted on the server, never returned to the client, and decrypted only inside the backend work that needs them.

That also changes what reliability can mean. A browser tab is a fragile place to run long AI work, especially on a phone. The Watai backend owns the generation path so a run can continue after the browser closes, then persist the result back into the thread. The client becomes a renderer and control surface rather than the thing keeping the work alive.

body.text: The assistant I wanted to use

body.markdown: Watai started with the core AI surfaces I expect from a modern assistant: chat, speech, image generation, thread history, markdown rendering, files, artifacts, settings, and sync. The repository also carries specs for a broader agentic direction: web search, file search, code interpreter, image generation tools, speech and transcription, deep research, and reusable agent skills.

items.heading: Server-run chat
items.text: Prompts create backend-owned runs, so responses can stream, sync, and finish independently of the tab.

items.heading: Image studio
items.text: Image generation is treated as a durable studio workflow, with server jobs, status cards, metadata, and a browsable gallery direction.

items.heading: Memory
items.text: The memory specs define a governed context layer: inspectable records, source-linked retrieval, background extraction, and user controls.

items.heading: Agent skills
items.text: The skills direction explores account-scoped skill packages that can mount instructions, references, scripts, and assets into code interpreter runs.

body.markdown: A private AI tool is not only about where the key lives. It also has to show what is configured, what is stored, what memory influenced a response, and how to correct or delete it. The memory work in Watai is deliberately governed: extraction is background work, retrieval is bounded, and the user-facing direction includes inspection, suppression, deletion, export, and source disclosure.

I also wanted the interface to feel calm. The onboarding is intentionally direct: connect the endpoint, choose the models, and opt into voice only if it is useful. The product can be technically ambitious underneath, but the setup should still feel like a personal tool, not an admin console.

Watai is public on GitHub at [github.com/prabinpebam/watai](https://github.com/prabinpebam/watai), and the live frontend is published at [prabinpebam.github.io/watai](https://prabinpebam.github.io/watai/).
